_about: College batch 11: COL_103 and the seven remaining senior scenes (113, 121, 123, 124, 126, 127, 130). Locked choices read the wrong-path flags (rebuilt_reputation, character_concerns, last_chance, online_incident), came_clean_tape (COL_121) and went_home_for_dad (COL_121).

scenarios.title: The Leadership Retreat
scenarios.text: The team's leaders spend a summer weekend at a lake house planning next season: team rules, goals, who sits where on the bus. It's also your only free weekend of the summer.

choices.label: Go and speak up
choices.result: You go and argue for one thing you care about: no freshman duties that aren't about football. It's in the rulebook by Sunday.

choices.label: Go and mostly listen
choices.result: You go, fish with the linemen and listen more than you talk. You come back knowing the team better than you did.

choices.label: Keep the weekend for yourself
choices.result: You skip it and spend the weekend doing nothing at all. You're rested, and you hear about the new rules secondhand.

choices.label: Run the meeting
choices.result: You've led a team before, so when the room stalls on Saturday, you take the whiteboard. The plan that comes out of it has your handwriting all over it.

scenarios.title: The Last Rivalry Week
scenarios.text: One last rivalry week. The younger players are watching the seniors to see what this week is supposed to look like, and somebody has already floated a midnight trip to the rival's campus.

choices.label: Set the tone in the film room
choices.result: You call a seniors-only film session and tell the younger players the rivalry gets settled on Saturday, not at midnight. The trip never happens.

choices.label: Plan something legal and loud
choices.result: You organize a pep rally banner and a team video instead. It's loud, it's fun, and nobody has to explain anything to anyone.

choices.label: Go on the midnight trip
choices.result: You pile into the car with the younger players. Campus security at the rival school takes down every name, and the first call the next morning goes to {coach}.

choices.label: Tell them what the long way back costs
choices.result: You tell the younger players about the six a.m. workouts and the community hours, and what one midnight trip cost you. Nobody gets in the car.
choices.lock_text: having taken the long way back

scenarios.title: The Little Brother's Recruiting
scenarios.text: {sibling} is a high school senior now, and college coaches are calling. He wants to know how to handle them, and he wants to know what you'd do differently.

choices.label: Tell him to be honest with every coach
choices.result: You tell him to be honest early, with every coach, even when it costs him an offer. He writes it down, which you've never seen him do.

choices.label: Make a list of his questions
choices.result: You build him a list of questions to ask every coach: who'll be his position coach, what happens if he's hurt, what the players really say. It takes a whole Sunday.

choices.label: Tell him the truth about your tape
choices.result: You tell {sibling} about the clip on your recruiting tape and what owning it taught you. He goes back and checks his own highlight video that night.
choices.lock_text: having owned up to your own recruiting tape

choices.label: Tell him what to ask about family
choices.result: You remind {sibling} of the night you flew home to the hospital, and tell him to ask every coach what happens when family needs you. Two coaches give answers he likes.
choices.lock_text: having gone home when {parent} was in the hospital

scenarios.title: The Last Injury Scare
scenarios.text: Your knee buckles on a routine practice kick three weeks before the scouts' workout. It holds, mostly. The trainer wants an MRI.

choices.label: Get the MRI today
choices.result: You get the scan the same afternoon. It's a sprain, not a tear, and you have a three-week plan before you leave the building.

choices.label: Wait until after the workout
choices.result: You ask to put off the scan until after the scouts come. You kick with a brace and a careful plant, and you don't sleep well.

choices.label: Say nothing and keep kicking
choices.result: You tell the trainer it was nothing and keep your full load. It holds for two weeks, and then it doesn't.

choices.label: Do what worked in high school
choices.result: You reported pain early once and it saved your season. You walk into the training room before practice ends and ask for the scan yourself.
choices.lock_text: having reported kicking pain early before

scenarios.title: Final Exams, Final Season
scenarios.text: Your last finals land in the same week as your last regular-season game. {teacher} has the exam schedule on the screen, and two of them are the morning after team travel.

choices.label: Study on the bus and the plane
choices.result: You turn every trip into a study session and get four hours of sleep a night. You pass everything, and you're exhausted on Saturday.

choices.label: Ask {teacher} to move two exams
choices.result: You ask {teacher} to arrange makeup times with your professors. It takes three emails each, and you get a normal week.

choices.label: Let the grades slide this once
choices.result: You do the minimum on two exams and focus on the last game. It's your senior year, and you don't regret it until the transcript arrives.

choices.label: Take every exam by the book
choices.result: You've been in front of an integrity panel once. You take every exam early, in the testing center, with nothing on the desk, and {teacher} notices without saying anything.
choices.lock_text: having sat through an integrity hearing

scenarios.title: The Exclusive Deal
scenarios.text: A national brand wants an exclusive NIL deal for your senior year. It pays more than everything else combined, it ends all your local deals, and the contract has a morality clause on page nine.

choices.label: Sign the exclusive deal
choices.result: You sign. The money is life-changing, and the local sandwich shop that sponsored you first takes your photo off the wall.

choices.label: Keep the local deals
choices.result: You turn it down and keep the deals with the people who backed you first. The sandwich shop names a sandwich after you.

choices.label: Ask your agent to negotiate
choices.result: You ask to keep one local deal as a condition. The brand says yes, for a little less money, and everyone gets something.

choices.label: Tell them about your record first
choices.result: You tell the brand about your college record before they find it themselves. They rewrite the morality clause and sign you anyway, for less, because you told them.
choices.lock_text: having a record the brand will find

scenarios.title: Giving Back
scenarios.text: Your hometown asks if you'd run a free kicking camp for kids this summer. It would cost you a week of draft training and some of your NIL money for the equipment.

choices.label: Run it, and pay for it
choices.result: You run the camp and buy every kid a ball with your name on it. Eighty kids show up, and {parent} works the check-in table.

choices.label: Run it, and find a sponsor
choices.result: You call the local businesses that backed you in high school. Two of them pay for everything, and you run the camp for free.

choices.label: Not this summer
choices.result: You say it'll have to wait until after the draft. They understand, and the camp happens without you.

choices.label: Bring in the people you volunteered with
choices.result: You call the people you did community work with, and they turn the camp into a weekend: a clinic, a cookout and a reading tent. It's the best week of your summer.
choices.lock_text: having put in community hours before

scenarios.title: The Old Posts
scenarios.text: Someone digs up posts from your first year of college, right in the middle of draft season. They're mean, they're stupid, and they're spreading.

choices.label: Post a short, real apology
choices.result: You write three sentences yourself: what you said, why it was wrong and who you are now. It's quoted everywhere, and the scouts mostly move on.

choices.label: Let the media staff handle it
choices.result: You hand it to the school's media staff, who write a careful statement for you. It's polished, and nobody believes you wrote it.

choices.label: Say they're taken out of context
choices.result: You post that the screenshots are fake and out of context. Someone posts the originals an hour later, with the dates.

choices.label: Go to {coach} before anyone asks
choices.result: You've been here before, so you walk into {coach}'s office with the screenshots before the coach sees them. You write the apology together.
choices.lock_text: having been through an online mess before
